passage: Linguist Wallace Chafe ______ argued that spoken language unfolds in short bursts called intonation units. These bursts roughly correspond to the limited focus of moment-to-moment consciousness, suggesting that even the grammatical structure of everyday talk is shaped by cognitive constraints on speaker attention rather than by purely linguistic rules.
question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: a longtime professor of linguistics at UC Santa Barbara,
, a longtime professor of linguistics at UC Santa Barbara
a longtime professor of linguistics at UC Santa Barbara
, a longtime professor of linguistics at UC Santa Barbara,

explanation: The correct answer is D, ", a longtime professor of linguistics at UC Santa Barbara,". The blank holds a nonrestrictive appositive — extra biographical information about Wallace Chafe that could be removed without changing which person the sentence is about, since "Wallace Chafe" already uniquely identifies him. Standard English requires a nonrestrictive appositive to be set off from the main clause by a matched pair of bracketing marks: paired commas, paired em-dashes, or paired parentheses. Because the inserted phrase contains no internal commas of its own, the lightest matched pair — paired commas — is the canonical choice. Choice D places a comma both before and after the appositive, cleanly opening and closing the insertion so the main clause "Linguist Wallace Chafe…argued that spoken language unfolds in short bursts…" reads through unbroken.

_meta.rule: paired commas around a nonrestrictive appositive (no internal commas)
_meta.anchor: Wallace Chafe — UC Santa Barbara linguist; intonation units / consciousness ('Discourse, Consciousness, and Time', 1994)

distractors.B: surface-match (opening comma only — looks like start of paired-comma pattern, missing close)
distractors.C: scope-shift (closing comma only — different rule: trailing-interrupter / list-tail comma)
distractors.D: inverse (no commas — treats appositive as restrictive)
